description: Inspect a residential kitchen, bathroom, and living area electrical installation for branch circuit code violations including GFCI/AFCI protection, receptacle spacing, wire sizing, and dedicated circuit requirements.
environmentDescription: A residential dwelling with exposed kitchen, bathroom, garage, bedroom, and living room electrical installations showing branch circuit wiring, receptacles, breakers, and conductors.

violations.description: Standard {term:receptacle} at bathroom sink without {term:shock-protection-device} protection

citations.text: In a home's bathrooms, every 125 V to 250 V receptacle needs GFCI protection.
A 5-15R or 5-20R receptacle within 1.5 m of a sink, bathtub or shower stall needs Class A GFCI protection.

violations.hintText: Check if bathroom outlets have {term:shock-protection-device} protection. Look for the TEST/RESET buttons on the {term:receptacle} face.
violations.inspectionNote: This bathroom {term:receptacle} lacks required {term:shock-protection-device} protection. Water proximity creates an electrocution hazard.

violations.description: Kitchen countertop receptacle lacks GFCI protection

citations.text: In a home's kitchens, every 125 V to 250 V receptacle needs GFCI protection, not only the ones that serve the countertop.
Socket-outlets rated up to 32 A on AC final circuits need additional protection from an RCD with a rated trip current of 30 mA or less.
citations.description: Kitchen worktop socket-outlet without RCD protection
citations.hintText: Socket-outlets up to 32 A need 30 mA RCD protection. Check the consumer unit for an RCD or RCBO on this circuit, or an RCD at the socket.
citations.inspectionNote: This kitchen socket-outlet has no 30 mA RCD protection.

violations.hintText: Kitchen countertop outlets need GFCI protection. Check for TEST/RESET buttons.
violations.inspectionNote: This kitchen countertop receptacle is missing required GFCI protection near water sources.

citations.text: Garages and outbuildings need GFCI protection on 125 V to 250 V receptacles when the floor is at or below grade.
Socket-outlets rated up to 32 A on AC final circuits need additional protection from an RCD with a rated trip current of 30 mA or less, including those used for mobile equipment outdoors.
citations.hintText: Socket-outlets up to 32 A need 30 mA RCD protection. Check the consumer unit for an RCD or RCBO on this circuit.
citations.inspectionNote: This garage socket-outlet has no 30 mA RCD protection.

violations.hintText: Garages at or below grade level require GFCI-protected outlets.
violations.inspectionNote: Garage receptacle at grade level is missing required GFCI protection.

violations.description: Wall receptacles spaced 14 feet apart, exceeding 12-foot maximum

citations.text: Place receptacles so every point along a wall's floor line is within 6 feet of one.
Place dwelling receptacles so that every spot along the floor line of usable wall space is within 1.8 m of one.
citations.description: Wall receptacles about 4.3 m (14 ft) apart, farther than the 3.6 m maximum
citations.hintText: No point along the floor line of usable wall space may be more than 1.8 m from a receptacle, so receptacles can be at most 3.6 m apart.
citations.inspectionNote: This wall section has a gap of about 4.3 m (14 ft) between receptacles, more than the 3.6 m that the 1.8 m rule allows.

violations.hintText: No point along a wall should be more than 6 feet from a receptacle. That means outlets must be no more than 12 feet apart.
violations.inspectionNote: This wall section has a 14-foot gap between receptacles, exceeding the 12-foot maximum spacing rule.

sceneFact.note: Distance from the farthest point along the wall line to the nearest receptacle. Twice this is the gap between two receptacles. The 14 ft gap puts the middle of the wall 7 ft from either receptacle.

violations.description: 14 AWG conductor connected to a 20-ampere breaker

citations.text: Small copper conductors have breaker limits: 15 A for 14 AWG, 20 A for 12 AWG and 30 A for 10 AWG.
A device protecting copper conductors from 14 AWG to 10 AWG is limited to 15 A for 14 AWG, 20 A for 12 AWG and 30 A for 10 AWG, and generally cannot be rated above the conductor's ampacity.

violations.hintText: Check the wire gauge against the breaker size. 14 AWG wire can only be on a 15-amp breaker.
violations.inspectionNote: 14 AWG wire is connected to a 20A breaker. This wire is rated for only 15A and could overheat under load.

violations.description: Bedroom branch circuit protected by standard breaker instead of AFCI

citations.text: In a home, 120 V single-phase 15 A and 20 A branch circuits that serve outlets in habitable rooms such as kitchens, living and dining rooms, bedrooms, closets, hallways and laundry areas need arc-fault protection by one of the methods in 210.12(A)(1) through (A)(6).

Branch circuits that supply 125 V receptacles rated 20 A or less in a dwelling need combination-type AFCI protection, with listed exemptions such as refrigerator, kitchen counter and bathroom receptacles.

violations.hintText: Bedroom circuits require arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI) protection at the panel.
violations.inspectionNote: This bedroom circuit uses a standard breaker. AFCI protection is required to prevent electrical fires from arc faults.

violations.description: Living room branch circuit missing AFCI protection at panel

citations.text: In a home, 120 V single-phase 15 A and 20 A branch circuits that serve outlets in habitable rooms such as kitchens, living and dining rooms, bedrooms, closets, hallways and laundry areas need arc-fault protection by one of the methods in 210.12(A)(1) through (A)(6).

Branch circuits that supply 125 V receptacles rated 20 A or less in a dwelling need combination-type AFCI protection, with listed exemptions such as refrigerator, kitchen counter and bathroom receptacles.
citations.inspectionNote: Living room circuit lacks AFCI protection. Combination-type AFCI protection is required for receptacle circuits in most dwelling living spaces.

violations.hintText: Living room circuits also require AFCI protection. Check the breaker type at the panel.
violations.inspectionNote: Living room circuit lacks AFCI protection. The code requires AFCI for virtually all dwelling unit living spaces.

violations.description: Kitchen countertop point 42 inches from the nearest receptacle, over the 24-inch limit

citations.text: Space countertop receptacles so that nowhere along the counter's back wall are you over 24 inches (horizontally) from one.
Behind kitchen counter work surfaces, install split receptacles so that you are never farther than 900 mm, measured along the wall line, from one.
citations.description: Kitchen countertop point 42 inches (about 1.07 m) from the nearest receptacle, over the 900 mm limit
citations.hintText: Along the counter wall line, no point may be more than 900 mm from a receptacle.
citations.inspectionNote: This countertop has an 84 inch (about 2.1 m) stretch with no receptacle, so its middle is about 1.07 m from the nearest one, over the 900 mm limit.

violations.hintText: Countertop receptacles must be within 24 inches of any point along the counter wall line.
violations.inspectionNote: This countertop has an 84-inch stretch with no receptacle, so its middle is 42 inches from the nearest one, over the 24-inch maximum.

sceneFact.note: Distance from the farthest point along the wall line to the nearest receptacle. Twice this is the gap between two receptacles. An 84 in stretch of counter with no receptacle puts its middle 42 in from the nearest one.

violations.description: Bathroom receptacle circuit shared with hallway, not a dedicated branch circuit

citations.text: Provide at least one 120 V, 20 A circuit for the bathroom receptacles.

violations.hintText: Bathroom receptacles require a dedicated 20A branch circuit. Check if the circuit also serves other rooms.
violations.inspectionNote: This breaker serves both bathroom and hallway outlets. Bathroom receptacles require a dedicated 20A branch circuit.

violations.description: Only one small-appliance branch circuit serving kitchen instead of required two

citations.text: Provide two or more 20 A small-appliance circuits for the kitchen receptacles.

violations.hintText: Kitchens require at least two 20A small-appliance branch circuits. Count the circuits at the panel.
violations.inspectionNote: Only one small-appliance circuit is provided for the kitchen. The code requires a minimum of two 20A circuits.

violations.description: Four NM cables bundled through single stud hole without ampacity derate

citations.text: Bundling more than two NM cables (each with at least two current-carrying conductors) in a single hole in wood framing, without any gap between them, calls for derating each conductor's ampacity per Table 310.15(C)(1).

violations.hintText: When multiple NM cables pass through the same hole, ampacity derating may be required.
violations.inspectionNote: Four NM cables are bundled through a single stud hole. With this many cables, ampacity must be derated per Table 310.15(C)(1), potentially making the conductors undersized for their breakers.

violations.description: Dishwasher branch circuit lacks GFCI protection

citations.text: The outlets that supply dishwashers in homes need GFCI protection, whether the dishwasher is plugged in or hard-wired.

violations.hintText: Dishwashers in homes need GFCI protection on the outlet that supplies them. Check the breaker or outlet type.

violations.description: Hallway receptacle circuit is fed by a plain breaker with no arc-fault protection

citations.text: In a dwelling unit, 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A branch circuits serving outlets or devices in hallways and the other listed areas need arc-fault protection by one of the means in 210.12(A), usually a combination-type {term:arc-fault-device}.

violations.hintText: Look at the {term:breaker} feeding the hallway outlets and read what is printed on it.
violations.inspectionNote: The hallway receptacle is fed from an ordinary breaker with no test button or arc-fault marking. The circuit should show an arc-fault device in the {term:panel}.

violations.description: Dining room receptacle circuit is protected by a standard breaker, not an arc-fault device

citations.text: Dining room outlets on 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A dwelling-unit circuits need arc-fault protection by one of the means in 210.12(A).

violations.hintText: Check the {term:breaker} for the circuit that serves the dining room wall outlets.
violations.inspectionNote: The breaker labelled for the dining room has no test button and no arc-fault marking. Compare it with a breaker that carries both.

violations.description: Family room receptacle circuit has only a standard breaker

citations.text: Family room outlets on 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A dwelling-unit circuits need arc-fault protection by one of the means in 210.12(A), not just overcurrent protection.

violations.hintText: Follow the family room outlets back to the {term:panel} and inspect the protective device.
violations.inspectionNote: The family room circuit lands on a plain single-pole breaker. There is no arc-fault test button or marking on its face.

violations.description: Walk-in closet receptacle is on a circuit with no arc-fault protection

citations.text: Closets are among the dwelling-unit areas where 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A circuits need arc-fault protection by one of the means in 210.12(A).

violations.hintText: Closets are easy to forget. Check what protects the circuit for this outlet.
violations.inspectionNote: A receptacle in the walk-in closet is supplied by a standard breaker. Nothing on the breaker or the receptacle shows arc-fault protection.

violations.description: Kitchen counter circuit has ground-fault protection only and no arc-fault protection

citations.text: Kitchen outlets on dwelling-unit 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A circuits need arc-fault protection by one of the means in 210.12(A), in addition to any ground-fault protection the counter location needs.

violations.hintText: The counter outlet is protected against one hazard. Ask whether it is protected against another.
violations.inspectionNote: The kitchen receptacle is a ground-fault type with test and reset buttons, fed by a plain breaker. The circuit has no arc-fault device at the {term:panel} or at the first outlet.

violations.description: Laundry area receptacle circuit has ground-fault protection only and no arc-fault protection

citations.text: Laundry areas are on the dwelling-unit list needing arc-fault protection for 120 V 10 A, 15 A and 20 A circuits, by one of the means in 210.12(A).

violations.hintText: Ground-fault protection is not the same as arc-fault protection. Check what protects this circuit.
violations.inspectionNote: The washer receptacle is supplied by a ground-fault device on a standard breaker with no arc-fault marking. Ground-fault protection alone does not meet the arc-fault requirement.

violations.description: New bedroom outlets were added to an existing circuit that still has a plain breaker

citations.text: When branch-circuit wiring serving the dwelling areas in 210.12(B) is modified, replaced or extended, the circuit needs arc-fault protection by a 210.12(A) means or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle outlet of the existing circuit. A short extension adding no outlets or devices is excepted.

violations.hintText: Look at a room added to the house later. What changed on the circuit that feeds it?
violations.inspectionNote: A bedroom addition adds two new receptacles on a long cable run from an older circuit that still uses a plain breaker. The run is more than 6 ft and adds outlets, so the short-extension exception does not apply.
